This bill sets up a legal framework for a national cancer screening register.
The register would collect, store, and report data for bowel and cervical screening programs, and send invitations and test kits.
The government allocated funding for the register in the 2015-16 Budget, and the business case was approved in the 2016-17 Budget.
Creates a legislative framework for the National Cancer Screening Register.
Authorises collection, use and disclosure of information for the register.
Requires certain persons to notify of unauthorised handling of personal information in the register.
The Australian Government, the Department of Human Services, State and Territory governments, and participants in bowel and cervical screening programs.

National Cancer Screening Register Bill 2016 and another - in Committee - Protection of private data
The speaker presented the National Cancer Screening Register Bill 2016 and its explanatory memorandum.

The National Cancer Screening Register Bill 2016 establishes a legislative framework for a national register to support the expanded National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (biennial screening for ages 50–74 by 2020) and the renewed National Cervical Screening Program (HPV test every five years from May 2017), aiming to improve early detection and reduce cancer deaths.

The bill provides consequential and transitional provisions to support the National Cancer Screening Register, authorising data collection and migration for cervical and bowel cancer screening, amending the FOI Act to unconditionally exempt protected personal information, and allowing a 12-month grace period for mandatory reporting until 1 May 2018.

Labor supported the policy intent of the bills to establish a National Cancer Screening Register but condemned the government for awarding a $220 million contract to Telstra four days before the 2016 election, before parliamentary approval. Labor proposed amendments to ensure the register is operated only by a government or not-for-profit entity, citing concerns over privacy, inadequate penalties, and Telstra's track record.

The speaker argued that the National Cancer Screening Register is important for improving cancer screening and prevention, but criticised the government's implementation as incompetent, including outsourcing to Telstra before legislation passed, privacy loopholes, and insufficient penalties. They proposed three amendments: limiting the operator to a not-for-profit or government agency, mandatory data breach notifications, and increased penalties for unauthorised disclosure.

The speaker argued the government mishandled the National Cancer Screening Register Bill 2016 by signing a $220 million contract with Telstra before parliamentary approval, and announced Labor will move amendments on data holder requirements, mandatory breach disclosure, and increased penalties—raising the maximum fine from $21,600 to $108,000 for individuals and $540,000 for corporations.

The National Cancer Screening Register Bill 2016 was debated, with the speaker noting that over 130,000 Australians will be diagnosed with cancer this year and nearly 47,000 will die from it; they emphasised the importance of screening, citing BreastScreen Queensland's work and that the mortality rate for breast cancer dropped from 17 to 11 per 100,000 between 1968 and 2013.

The Labor MP criticised the government for signing a $220 million contract with Telstra to outsource the National Cancer Screening Register before the legislation was debated in parliament, arguing this jeopardised privacy protections for highly sensitive health data like cancer diagnoses and HPV status. She also condemned the government's failure to introduce mandatory data breach notification laws, warning the register's outsourcing to a private firm threatened universal healthcare and could deter people from getting screened.

The speaker opposed the National Cancer Screening Register Bill 2016, arguing the contract awarded to Telstra Health—a private, for-profit company with limited health experience—lacked transparency and should instead be run by a government or not-for-profit entity.

The speaker supported the National Cancer Screening Register Bill and Labor's amendments to limit operation to a not-for-profit or government agency, arguing that the register would prevent an estimated 140 cervical cancers and 300–500 bowel cancer deaths per year, but criticised the government for awarding the contract to Telstra before the legislation passed and for outsourcing sensitive health data to a multinational for-profit corporation.

The National Cancer Screening Register Bill 2016 establishes a legislative framework for a national register to support the National Cervical Screening Program from 1 May 2016 and expand the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program, with capacity for future expansion to other cancer screening programs.

The opposition moved amendments to restrict the National Cancer Screening Register to permitted entities such as government departments, public bodies and charitable organisations, arguing that a for-profit company should not hold sensitive health data under a $200 million contract signed before the election.
